comparisons.peer_topic: Noninterest expense increase drivers and prior year comparisons
comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people, operations, and technology, partially offset by higher FDIC expense in 2023 (including a $2.1 billion special assessment) and lower expenses from a liquidating business activity.
comparisons.comparison: While Citigroup's expenses decreased 2% due to restructuring benefits, Bank of America's noninterest expense increased by $967 million (to $66.8 billion). Both companies, however, cited investments in technology and people/operations as components of their expense profiles, though for BAC these were net increase drivers rather than offsetting factors for a broader decrease. BAC also noted a benefit from lower FDIC expenses compared to the prior year, whereas Citi's disclosure did not highlight FDIC special assessment impacts as a primary driver in the same sentence.

sentences.text: Expenses decreased 2%, mainly driven by benefits from prior repositioning and restructuring actions, partially offset by higher volume-related expenses and technology investments focused on risk and controls and platform enhancements.
Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023.

The increase was primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses as well as investments in people, operations and technology, partially offset by higher Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) expense in 2023, including $2.1 billion for the estimated special assessment amount arising from the closure of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, and lower expenses related to a liquidating business activity.

comparisons.peer_summary: Operating expenses decreased 2% to $33.77 billion in 2024, aided by lower CIE commercial real estate impairments and prior year one-time charges like the GreenSky write-down, partially offset by higher compensation and transaction expenses, resulting in an efficiency ratio improvement to 63.1% from 74.6%.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup and Goldman Sachs reported a 2% decrease in expenses (or operating expenses) for 2024. However, the drivers differed: Citigroup attributed the decrease to benefits from prior repositioning and restructuring, while Goldman Sachs cited lower commercial real estate CIE impairments and prior year one-time charges (like the GreenSky write-down) as the primary drivers for the reduction, partially offset by higher compensation and transaction expenses in both cases.

sentences.text: Expenses decreased 2%, mainly driven by benefits from prior repositioning and restructuring actions, partially offset by higher volume-related expenses and technology investments focused on risk and controls and platform enhancements.

Operating expenses were $33.77 billion for 2024, 2% lower than 2023, reflecting decreases driven by significantly lower expenses, including impairments, related to commercial real estate in consolidated investment entities (CIEs) and other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including the write-down of identifiable intangible assets related to GreenSky Holdings, LLC (GreenSky), an impairment of goodwill related to Consumer platforms and the FDIC special assessment fee.
These decreases were partially offset by higher compensation and benefits expenses (reflecting improved operating performance) and higher transaction based expenses.

comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense was $35.4 billion, up 4%, driven by higher compensation expense (including revenue-related compensation and increased headcount) and higher technology and brokerage expense, partially offset by lower legal expense.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup reported a 2% decrease in expenses, driven by restructuring benefits, whereas JPMorgan Chase reported a 4% increase in noninterest expense to $35.4 billion. Both firms cited higher technology expense as a factor, but for JPM it was a driver of the increase, while for Citi it was a partial offset to the overall decrease. Additionally, JPM's increase was driven by higher compensation and headcount, whereas Citi's decrease was driven by restructuring actions.
